CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRESCRIBING__Saf:
Overview — Safe Prescribing & Prescribing Errors
The practical/clinical-governance counterpart to the prescribing-safety cluster: how to prescribe safely and why errors happen + how to prevent them.
The guiding philosophy: errors are usually a systems failure, not individual incompetence — the safe-prescribing response is to fix the system, not just blame the person.
Two halves: the principles of good prescribing (proactive) and the anatomy of prescribing errors (what goes wrong + prevention). Cross-ref: PK/PD, ADRs/Yellow Card, renal/hepatic dose adjustment, drugs in pregnancy, anticoagulation/insulin/steroids.
The Principles of Good Prescribing
Before prescribing, work through (Oxford "10 principles" distilled):
  • Clarify the indication — is a drug actually needed?
  • Take a full drug history — current + recent meds, incl. OTC + herbal; medication reconciliation
  • Check allergies + prior ADRs — avoid recurrence
  • Consider patient factors — age, pregnancy, renal/hepatic/cardiac function, genetics, comorbidity
  • Check interactions — you can't know them all → look them up (BNF)
  • Choose effective, safe, cost-effective drugs — right drug, dose, route, frequency, duration
  • Share the decision — patient ideas/concerns/expectations, informed consent
  • Write the prescription clearly (legible, generic names, no dangerous abbreviations)
  • Monitor + review — efficacy, ADRs, when to stop; deprescribe where appropriate
Use generic (non-proprietary) names — reduces confusion + reconciliation errors.
Writing a Safe Prescription
📷 Image placeholder — Correctly written drug-chart entry — generic name in CAPITALS, “micrograms”/“units” in full, no trailing zero, leading zero (0.5 not .5), with route/frequency/allergy box — beside common dangerous-abbreviation errors
The dangerous-abbreviation rules (high-yield / PSA)
  • Write "micrograms"/"nanograms" in full — never "mcg"/"µg" (misread as mg)
  • Write "units" in full — never "U" (misread as a zero → 10× insulin overdose)
  • No trailing zeros ("2 mg" not "2.0 mg"); leading zero for <1 ("0.5 mg" not ".5 mg")
  • Legible, in ink, signed + dated; generic name in CAPITALS
  • Route, frequency, duration/quantity; max dose for PRN; allergy status documented
  • Controlled drugs: additional legal requirements (dose in words + figures, total quantity)
Classifying Prescribing Errors

Type Definition

SlipRight plan, wrong action (attention lapse) — e.g. writing the wrong dose by accident

ViolationDeliberate deviation from a known rule
High-Risk Medications
"A PINCH" — the drugs causing disproportionate harm: Anti-infectives, Potassium, Insulin, Narcotics (opioids), Chemotherapy/anticoagulants, Heparin (+ sedatives).
  • Insulin ("U" misread → 10× dose)
  • Anticoagulants (warfarin/heparin → bleeding)
  • Opioids (respiratory depression)
  • Methotrexate — weekly not daily (a classic fatal error)
  • Potassium — never IV bolus (cross-ref electrolytes)
  • Gentamicin/vancomycin — need TDM
These need extra checks, monitoring, and often double-checking (e.g. insulin, chemo).
Why Errors Happen — the Systems Approach
The Swiss cheese model (Reason): errors result from multiple latent system failures lining up, not a single person's mistake — defences have "holes" that occasionally align.
  • Contributing factors: inadequate knowledge/training, incomplete drug history (~30% of errors), poor communication/handover, fatigue + workload (on-call prescribing), look-alike/sound-alike drugs, trade names, distraction
  • The "no-blame" / "just culture": focus on what went wrong (system) not who — encourages reporting + learning rather than concealment
Preventing Errors — system-level safeguards
Medication reconciliation — the single most effective intervention
Especially at admission/discharge transitions. Three steps: verify (accurate drug history) → clarify (appropriate drugs/doses) → reconcile (document changes). Pharmacist-led reconciliation is most effective.
  • Medication review + deprescribing (esp. polypharmacy/elderly — Beers criteria / STOPP-START for inappropriate prescribing in the elderly)
  • Electronic prescribing (ePMA) with decision support (interaction/allergy/dose alerts)
  • Double-checking high-risk drugs; standardised processes; BNF/protocols
  • Reporting + learning: incident reporting (Datix), the Yellow Card scheme for ADRs (cross-ref), Never Events (e.g. wrong-route chemo, insulin overdose from abbreviation) — wholly preventable serious incidents

Overview — ADRs & Yellow Card
📷 Image placeholder — Yellow Card thresholds — black-triangle ▼ drugs/vaccines/biosimilars: report ALL suspected reactions; established drugs: report all SERIOUS reactions (plus all in children and pregnancy)
ADR = a noxious + unintended response to a drug at normal therapeutic doses — distinct from overdose/toxicity, and from medication errors.
Two organising frameworks
  • How do we classify ADRs? — Rawlins-Thompson A–E
  • How do we report them? — the Yellow Card scheme
Cross-ref: PK/PD & drug interactions (mechanisms — this note's parent topic), toxicology (overdose — distinct from ADR), safe prescribing, hypersensitivity (type B immune ADRs).
Definitions — get the distinctions straight
  • ADR = harmful, unintended response at normal doses (≠ overdose)
  • Side effect = a known, often predictable secondary effect (a subset of ADRs)
  • Adverse drug event = any harm associated with a drug, including from medication error (broader)
Serious ADR (MHRA definition): one that is fatal, life-threatening, disabling/incapacitating, causes/prolongs hospitalisation, causes a congenital abnormality, or is otherwise medically significant.
The Rawlins-Thompson Classification (A–E)
📷 Image placeholder — Rawlins-Thompson types — A augmented/dose-related (usually dose-adjust), B bizarre/immune (STOP + avoid), C chronic, D delayed, E end-of-use/withdrawal (+ F failure)
Type Name Features Examples
AAugmented (commonest)Dose-dependent, predictable, exaggeration of the drug's action; low mortalityβ-blocker → bradycardia; opioid → resp depression; insulin → hypoglycaemia; anticoagulant → bleeding
BBizarre (2nd commonest)NOT dose-dependent, unpredictable, often immune-mediated; high mortalityPenicillin anaphylaxis, malignant hyperthermia, carbamazepine → SJS, Reye's (aspirin)
CChronic/ContinuedDose + time-dependent, with prolonged useSteroids → osteoporosis/Cushing's, bisphosphonates → osteonecrosis of jaw
DDelayedAppears long after exposureTeratogenesis (thalidomide), carcinogenesis, tardive dyskinesia
EEnd-of-use (withdrawal)On stopping (esp. abrupt)Steroid withdrawal → adrenal crisis, benzodiazepine/opioid withdrawal, β-blocker rebound
Mnemonic — ABCDE: Augmented, Bizarre, Chronic, Delayed, End-of-use. (Some add F = Failure of therapy — e.g. reduced efficacy from a drug interaction.)
The key split: Type A = predictable + dose-dependent (the bulk — manage by dose adjustment); Type B = unpredictable + immune (often need to stop + avoid the drug — cross-ref hypersensitivity).
Risk Factors for ADRs
  • Extremes of age (elderly + neonates — altered PK)
  • Polypharmacy (interaction risk)
  • Organ impairment (renal/hepatic — cross-ref dose adjustment)
  • Female sex
  • Genetic factors (CYP polymorphisms, G6PD)
  • Multiple comorbidities
Recognising & Assessing an ADR
  • Causality assessment: temporal relationship to starting the drug, known reaction profile, improvement on stopping (dechallenge) and recurrence on restarting (rechallenge), exclusion of other causes; formalised by scales (Naranjo)
  • High-yield "classic culprits": ACE inhibitors → cough/angioedema, statins → myopathy, amiodarone → multi-organ, methotrexate → marrow/liver (and the drugs flagged across the DILI / anticoagulation / steroid notes)
The Yellow Card Scheme
Run by the MHRA (+ Commission on Human Medicines) — the UK system for post-marketing pharmacovigilance (drug-safety surveillance after licensing), since 1964. Clinical trials are too small/short to detect rare or delayed ADRs → real-world reporting detects new safety signals.
  • Who can report: anyone — doctors, pharmacists, nurses, and patients/carers (voluntary; no proof of causation needed — report on suspicion)
Always report Detail
ALL suspected ADRs to "black triangle" (▼) drugsNew drugs/vaccines under additional monitoring — report any reaction, however minor
ALL serious suspected ADRs to established drugsEven if the reaction is already well-recognised
ALL suspected ADRs in children (<18)Even if the drug is off-label
Suspected ADRs in pregnancyHowever minor
Delayed reactions (cancers, fibrosis)Even years later
What's reportable: reactions to any therapeutic agent — prescribed and OTC/self-medication, vaccines, blood products, radiographic contrast, herbal/complementary products.
How: online (mhra.gov.uk/yellowcard), the Yellow Card app, via clinical IT systems, or paper forms in the back of the BNF.
The black triangle (▼): marks newly-licensed drugs/vaccines (and biosimilars) under intensive/additional monitoring; appears in the BNF + SmPC/PIL → report all reactions to these.
Minimising ADRs — the prescribing-safety link
  • Take a full drug + allergy history (incl. OTC/herbal)
  • Avoid polypharmacy (deprescribe); check interactions (BNF)
  • Start low, go slow in the elderly/organ impairment; use the fewest drugs
  • Monitor high-risk drugs; document + communicate allergies/reactions
  • Medication reconciliation at transitions of care (cross-ref safe prescribing)

Overview — Pain Management & Analgesia
The framework for analgesic prescribing: assess the pain → classify it → treat by the WHO ladder + by mechanism → prescribe opioids safely.
Classification 1 — Acute vs Chronic
Chronic = >3 months.
Classification 2 — Nociceptive vs Neuropathic
Different drugs — opioids work poorly on neuropathic pain.
Cross-ref: palliative care (palliative-specific opioid dosing/conversion/syringe drivers live there — this is the general framework), toxicology (opioid overdose → naloxone), PK/PD (opioid metabolism), MSK/neurology (chronic pain conditions).
Pain Assessment
  • Pain is subjective — measured by the patient's report: Visual Analogue Scale (VAS) and Numerical Rating Scale (NRS, 0–10)
  • SOCRATES for characterising pain; DN4 questionnaire (≥4/10 → neuropathic)
  • Assess impact (function, sleep, mood) — pain is biopsychosocial
Classifying Pain — directs the treatment
Type Mechanism Character Responds to
NociceptiveTissue damage → nociceptor activationAching, throbbing, well-localisedWHO ladder (paracetamol/NSAIDs/opioids)
NeuropathicNerve damage/dysfunctionBurning, shooting, tingling, allodyniaNeuropathic agents (opioids work poorly)
AcuteRecent, protective, self-limiting—Treat the cause + WHO ladder
Chronic>3 months—Multimodal; chronic primary pain → avoid most analgesia
The WHO Analgesic Ladder
📷 Image placeholder — WHO analgesic ladder — Step 1 non-opioid (paracetamol ± NSAID), Step 2 weak opioid (codeine/tramadol), Step 3 strong opioid (morphine/oxycodone/fentanyl), ± adjuvant at every step
Originally for cancer pain, now applied to acute + chronic pain; step up until pain controlled.
Step Pain Drugs
1MildNon-opioid: paracetamol ± NSAID (± adjuvant)
2ModerateWeak opioid: codeine, dihydrocodeine, tramadol (+ non-opioid ± adjuvant)
3SevereStrong opioid: morphine, oxycodone, fentanyl (+ non-opioid ± adjuvant)
The principles — "by the mouth, by the clock, by the ladder, for the individual": oral route preferred, regular dosing (not just PRN) for continuous pain, step-wise, individualised. Leapfrogging allowed — severe pain → start at Step 3 directly; breakthrough pain → fast-acting rescue dose.
Step 4 (modern addition): interventional — nerve blocks, spinal analgesia, spinal cord stimulation.
The opioid-crisis caveat: the ladder drove opioid overuse in chronic non-cancer pain; weak opioids (Step 2) add little and modern practice questions them.
The Analgesics by Class
Drug/class Mechanism Key cautions
ParacetamolCentral (poorly understood)Hepatotoxic in overdose (cross-ref toxicology); dose-reduce in liver disease/low weight
NSAIDsInhibit COX → ↓prostaglandinsGI ulcer/bleed, renal impairment, CVD, asthma; avoid in CKD/PUD/heart failure (co-prescribe PPI if needed)
Weak opioids (codeine, tramadol)µ-opioid agonist; codeine is a prodrug → morphine (CYP2D6)Codeine ineffective in poor metabolisers, dangerous in ultra-rapid metabolisers; tramadol also lowers seizure threshold + serotonergic
Strong opioids (morphine, oxycodone, fentanyl)µ-opioid agonistSee opioid section below
Opioid Prescribing & Safety
ALWAYS co-prescribe a laxative (stimulant ± softener) — constipation is near-universal; consider a PRN antiemetic when starting.
  • Side effects: constipation (near-universal), nausea (often transient), drowsiness, respiratory depression, pruritus, tolerance + dependence
  • Opioid toxicity: drowsiness → confusion, pinpoint pupils, myoclonus, respiratory depression → reduce dose / rotate opioid; naloxone only if life-threatening (cross-ref toxicology)
  • Renal impairment: morphine accumulates (active metabolites) → use oxycodone, or fentanyl/buprenorphine (cross-ref renal dose adjustment)
Patient-controlled analgesia (PCA)
IV strong opioid, patient-triggered, locked to prevent overdose; needs anaesthetic input + naloxone/antiemetic/atropine available; avoid other PRN opioids alongside.
Opioid patches (background analgesia)
Buprenorphine, fentanyl — for stable chronic pain, not acute titration.
Palliative-specific dosing (breakthrough = 1/6 daily dose, oral→SC conversions) lives in the palliative care note.
Neuropathic Pain — different drugs
📷 Image placeholder — NICE CG173 neuropathic pain first-line — one of amitriptyline, duloxetine, gabapentin or pregabalin; switch if one fails; carbamazepine for trigeminal neuralgia
Opioids work poorly — use specific agents. NICE first-line (choose one of four): amitriptyline, duloxetine, gabapentin, or pregabalin (switch if one fails).
  • Tramadol as rescue only; capsaicin cream for localised; carbamazepine for trigeminal neuralgia specifically
  • Causes: diabetic neuropathy, post-herpetic neuralgia, nerve impingement, MS, trigeminal neuralgia
Adjuvants
Drugs not primarily analgesic but useful in specific pain:
  • Antidepressants (amitriptyline, duloxetine — neuropathic)
  • Anticonvulsants (gabapentin/pregabalin — neuropathic)
  • Corticosteroids (inflammatory / nerve compression / raised ICP)
  • Bisphosphonates (bone pain)
  • Benzodiazepines (muscle spasm), antispasmodics
Chronic Pain Principles — the NICE exam point
Chronic primary pain (no underlying cause — e.g. fibromyalgia): NICE recommends avoiding most analgesia (paracetamol/NSAIDs/opioids/gabapentinoids) → instead exercise, psychological therapy (CBT/ACT), and consider an antidepressant (duloxetine) — the high-yield SBA.
  • Chronic secondary pain (underlying cause): treat the cause + multimodal analgesia
  • Multimodal/biopsychosocial: physiotherapy, psychology, pain clinic; minimise long-term opioids (limited benefit + harms in chronic non-cancer pain)
Specific Contexts
  • Post-operative: regular paracetamol + NSAID + opioid (regular MR + PRN immediate-release); local anaesthetic wound infiltration; PCA; reduce as recovering
  • Acute severe pain: titrated IV opioid

Overview — Renal / Hepatic Dose Adjustment Principles
📷 Image placeholder — Child-Pugh score — the 5 components (bilirubin, albumin, INR, ascites, encephalopathy) and A/B/C grading
The kidneys and liver are the two main routes of drug elimination — kidney = excretion (water-soluble drugs + metabolites), liver = metabolism. Impair either and drugs/active metabolites accumulate → toxicity.
Two decisive questions for any drug in organ impairment
  • How is it cleared — renal vs hepatic?
  • How narrow is its therapeutic window?
Together these determine whether dose adjustment matters.
A principles note — the BNF appendices hold the per-drug detail; the examinable skill is the reasoning + recognising the classic dangerous drugs. Cross-ref: AKI/CKD, DILI, anticoagulation, PK/PD, toxicology.
Pharmacokinetic Framework — the ADME lens
ADME step Affected by Consequence
AbsorptionGut oedema, altered first-passVariable bioavailability
Distribution↓albumin (liver/nephrotic)More free (active) drug for protein-bound drugs
MetabolismLiver impairment↓clearance of hepatically-metabolised drugs
ExcretionKidney impairment↓clearance of renally-excreted drugs
The core mechanism: impairment → ↓clearance → ↑plasma level + prolonged half-life → accumulation → toxicity, unless dose/interval is adjusted.
Renal Dose Adjustment
📷 Image placeholder — DOAC renal thresholds — apixaban/rivaroxaban/edoxaban (avoid <15) vs dabigatran (contraindicated <30) by CrCl
  • Who's at risk: drugs that are renally excreted (especially unchanged), have active renally-cleared metabolites, and/or a narrow therapeutic index
  • How you adjust: reduce the dose and/or lengthen the dosing interval; some drugs are contraindicated below a certain eGFR
Assessing function for dosing: eGFR is the usual measure, but some dosing (DOACs, aminoglycosides, digoxin) traditionally uses creatinine clearance (Cockcroft-Gault); eGFR is unreliable in AKI (not at steady state) and at extremes of body habitus.
Drug Why / what happens
Aminoglycosides (gentamicin)Nephrotoxic + ototoxic; renally cleared → monitor levels (check after 3 doses)
VancomycinNephrotoxic, narrow window → TDM
MetforminAccumulates → lactic acidosis; stop if eGFR low/AKI
LithiumNarrow window → toxicity → TDM
DigoxinNarrow window → toxicity → TDM
DOACs / LMWHAccumulate → bleeding (apixaban avoid <15 (caution 15–29), rivaroxaban avoid <15 mL/min)
Opioids — morphineActive renally-excreted metabolite accumulates → toxicity → use oxycodone instead
Methotrexate, allopurinol, many antibioticsRenally cleared → reduce/avoid
Nephrotoxic drugs to STOP in AKI — "AADN": ACEi/ARB, Aminoglycosides, Diuretics, NSAIDs (cross-ref AKI). The "may need to stop" list (metformin, lithium, digoxin) also applies.
Hepatic Dose Adjustment — the trickier one
Why it's harder than renal: there's no "eGFR for the liver" — use clinical severity (Child-Pugh), LFTs, and synthetic function (albumin, INR, bilirubin) as a guide, rather than a clean number to dose against.
Mechanism Effect on dosing
↓ first-pass metabolism↑ bioavailability of orally-administered, highly-extracted drugs → effectively higher dose
↓ drug-metabolising enzymesReduced clearance of hepatically-metabolised drugs → accumulation
↓ albumin synthesisMore free (active) drug for highly protein-bound drugs
↓ clotting factor synthesisExaggerated anticoagulant effect (warfarin)
Portosystemic shuntingDrugs bypass hepatic metabolism; risk of precipitating hepatic encephalopathy
Drug Concern
ParacetamolDose-dependent hepatotoxicity (reduce in severe liver disease)
StatinsHepatotoxic → LFT monitoring (check at 3 + 12 months)
WarfarinExaggerated effect (↓clotting factor synthesis)
Sedatives / opioids / benzodiazepinesPrecipitate hepatic encephalopathy — use cautiously
Methotrexate, valproate, amiodaroneHepatotoxic (cross-ref DILI)
Anti-TB (isoniazid/rifampicin/pyrazinamide)Hepatotoxic (cross-ref DILI)
Avoid/use cautiously in liver disease (esp. cirrhosis): sedating drugs (encephalopathy), constipating drugs (constipation precipitates encephalopathy), NSAIDs (fluid retention → worsen ascites + hepatorenal syndrome, GI bleed), and hepatotoxins.
General Safe-Prescribing Principles in Organ Impairment
  • Start low, go slow — lowest effective dose, titrate cautiously
  • Avoid nephrotoxic/hepatotoxic drugs where an alternative exists
  • Monitor: organ function + therapeutic drug monitoring (TDM) for narrow-index drugs
  • Check the BNF — dedicated renal + hepatic impairment appendices for specific drugs
  • Review the whole drug chart in any patient with new organ impairment (medicines reconciliation)

Kidney = excretion, liver = metabolism; impairment → accumulation → toxicity.

Overview — Drugs to Avoid in Pregnancy
A high-yield prescribing-safety reference: which drugs are teratogenic/harmful, what specific fetal harm each causes (the examinable pairing), and the safe alternative to switch to.
Two organising principles
  • Timing matters: the 1st trimester (organogenesis) is most vulnerable to structural malformations; some drugs (ACEi, NSAIDs) harm specifically in the 2nd/3rd trimester
  • Always ask "could she be pregnant?" before prescribing in any woman of childbearing age, and switch teratogenic drugs pre-conception where possible
Cross-ref: anticoagulation (warfarin→LMWH), epilepsy/antiepileptics, UTIs in pregnancy (antibiotic timing).

  • Always check pregnancy status before prescribing teratogens to women of childbearing potential

Overview — Steroid Equivalents & Sick Day Rules

Two linked safe-prescribing concepts, both flowing from the HPA axis: steroid equivalents (converting between corticosteroids — they differ in glucocorticoid potency, mineralocorticoid effect, and duration) and sick day rules (adjusting dose during illness/stress).
The unifying physiology: exogenous steroids → negative feedback → HPA suppression → adrenal glands stop making cortisol → patient can't respond to physiological stress → risk of adrenal (Addisonian) crisis.
Cross-ref: Addison's / adrenal insufficiency (the crisis), Cushing's (steroid excess), the steroid side-effect profile, safe prescribing.
Steroid Equivalents
The key glucocorticoids differ on three axes: glucocorticoid (anti-inflammatory) potency, mineralocorticoid (salt/water) effect, and duration.

Hydrocortisone20 mgHigh (salt-retaining)ShortAdrenal replacement (mimics cortisol); IV in crisis

Rough rule: ~10 mg hydrocortisone ≈ 2.5 mg prednisolone ≈ 0.375 mg dexamethasone → prednisolone ≈ 4× hydrocortisone potency; dexamethasone is most potent (~25–30×) and longest-acting.
The mineralocorticoid logic — why the choice matters
  • Hydrocortisone — significant salt-retaining activity → used in adrenal insufficiency (you want that effect) and in crisis (IV)
  • Dexamethasone — negligible mineralocorticoid effect → chosen where fluid retention would harm (raised ICP / cerebral oedema); long duration suits single daily dosing
Physiological replacement dose ≈ hydrocortisone 15–25 mg/day in divided doses.
HPA Axis Suppression — the rationale
  • Mechanism: exogenous glucocorticoids suppress hypothalamic CRH + pituitary ACTH → adrenal atrophy → endogenous cortisol production stops
  • Who is at risk (NHS Steroid Emergency Card threshold): anyone on prednisolone ≥5 mg/day (or equivalent) for ≥4 weeks — across ALL routes (oral, inhaled, topical, intranasal); also high-dose inhaled (beclometasone >1000 mcg/day or fluticasone >500 mcg/day)
  • The consequence: a suppressed patient cannot increase cortisol in response to stress (illness, surgery, trauma) → without extra steroid → adrenal crisis
NHS Steroid Emergency Card: issued to at-risk patients so any treating clinician knows they need stress-dose cover.
Sick Day Rules
The principle: physiological stress normally triples-or-more cortisol output; the suppressed patient must take this extra steroid exogenously.
Situation Action
Minor illness / no feverUsual dose (no change)
Illness WITH fever / moderate illnessDouble the usual oral dose for the duration of illness
Already on prednisolone ≥10–15 mg/dayNo additional sick-day dosing needed (already above stress threshold)
Vomiting / can't keep tablets downEmergency parenteral (IM/IV) hydrocortisone + seek urgent help
Persistent vomiting / diarrhoea999 / Emergency Department — risk of crisis

During significant stress, give at least 40 mg oral hydrocortisone/day in divided doses (or ≥10 mg oral prednisolone/day) until the illness resolves.
Patient-safety message: carry the Steroid Emergency Card, double the dose when febrile, and switch to injection if vomiting.
Adrenal Crisis — the emergency the rules prevent
Presentation
Hypotension/shock, vomiting, abdominal pain, hypoglycaemia, hyponatraemia/hyperkalaemia, reduced consciousness — in a steroid-dependent patient who is ill, stressed, or has missed doses.
Management (don't wait to confirm): 100 mg IM/IV hydrocortisone immediately, then 200 mg/24h infusion (or 50 mg 6-hourly) + IV 0.9% saline + treat hypoglycaemia.
Steroid Withdrawal / Tapering — the flip side
Never stop long-term steroids abruptly — the suppressed axis can't immediately resume cortisol production → precipitates adrenal insufficiency.
  • Taper gradually to let the HPA axis recover — especially after >3 weeks of treatment, high doses, or repeated courses
  • Below physiological-equivalent doses, hydrocortisone's shorter half-life may aid recovery; expect temporary withdrawal symptoms (fatigue, low appetite, low mood)
  • Other reason not to stop abruptly: rebound of the underlying disease

Heparins — UFH & LMWH
Mechanism: activate antithrombin III → inactivate thrombin + factor Xa.
LMWH (enoxaparin, dalteparin) — the workhorse

  • Uses: VTE prophylaxis (standard inpatient thromboprophylaxis), treatment-dose acute VTE, ACS, bridging, pregnancy (safe — doesn't cross placenta)
  • Renal caution: renally cleared → avoid/reduce in severe renal impairment (use UFH instead)

  • Mechanism: inhibits vitamin K epoxide reductase (VKORC1) → reduces vitamin-K-dependent factors II, VII, IX, X (and proteins C & S)
  • Monitoring: INR (target 2–3 for most; 2.5–3.5 for mechanical valves) — narrow therapeutic window

Metabolism — P450 → huge interaction burden

Pharmacokinetics — ADME
📷 Image placeholder — First-order vs zero-order elimination — exponential decline (constant fraction) vs linear decline to plateau (constant amount, the PASTA drugs), with the disproportionate level rise on small dose increases
Absorption
  • Bioavailability (F) = AUC(oral) / AUC(IV). IV = 100% by definition.
  • Factors: drug solubility/charge, gut pH, blood flow, transit time
  • First-pass metabolism: oral drugs metabolised in gut wall + liver before reaching systemic circulation. High first-pass = low oral bioavailability (morphine, nitrates, propranolol, TCAs)
  • Buccal/sublingual: bypass first-pass metabolism (GTN, buprenorphine)
Distribution
  • Volume of distribution (Vd) = dose / plasma concentration
  • Low Vd → stays in plasma (heparin, warfarin — highly protein-bound)
  • High Vd → distributes widely into tissues (amiodarone, chloroquine, digoxin)
  • Factors: protein binding (albumin), lipid solubility, tissue affinity, BBB, placenta
Metabolism
  • Phase 1: catabolic (oxidation, reduction, hydrolysis) — CYP450 enzymes. Converts drug to more polar metabolite.
  • Phase 2: anabolic (conjugation — glucuronidation, sulfation, acetylation). Produces water-soluble conjugate for renal excretion.
  • Some drugs are prodrugs: converted to active form (codeine → morphine, azathioprine → 6-MP)
Elimination
First-Order Kinetics (95% of drugs)
  • Rate of elimination proportional to concentration
  • Constant fraction eliminated per unit time
  • 4–5 half-lives to reach steady state
  • 5 half-lives = <5% drug remaining
Zero-Order Kinetics (saturated enzymes)
  • Constant amount eliminated per unit time (independent of concentration)
  • Metabolic pathway saturated → no proportional increase
  • Examples: PASTA — Phenytoin, Aspirin (high dose), Salicylates, Theophylline, Alcohol
Loading vs maintenance dose: the loading dose depends on Vd (fills the volume of distribution); the maintenance dose depends on clearance (replaces what's eliminated). Loading dose bypasses the 4–5 half-life wait for rapid effect.
Therapeutic Index & Therapeutic Drug Monitoring (TDM)
Therapeutic index (TI) = ratio of toxic dose to effective dose. Narrow TI = small margin between effective and toxic → needs monitoring. This is the why behind zero-order phenytoin, the digoxin interactions, and gentamicin levels.
Narrow-TI drugs requiring TDM
Digoxin, lithium, phenytoin, theophylline, gentamicin/vancomycin, warfarin (INR), ciclosporin/tacrolimus.
CYP450 Interactions — Clinically Critical
CYP450 Inducers (↑ enzyme → ↓ drug level)
  • CRAPS: Carbamazepine, Rifampicin, Alcohol (chronic), Phenytoin, Smoking (+ St John's Wort)
  • Effect: reduce efficacy of warfarin, COCP, statins, corticosteroids, ciclosporin
  • OCP: rifampicin and carbamazepine render the pill ineffective — use alternative contraception
CYP450 Inhibitors (↓ enzyme → ↑ drug level)
  • Antibiotics: ciprofloxacin, erythromycin/clarithromycin
  • Amiodarone, allopurinol, grapefruit juice (intestinal CYP3A4)
  • Isoniazid, omeprazole, sodium valproate
  • SSRIs (sertraline, fluoxetine)
  • Acute alcohol
  • Effect: ↑ toxicity of warfarin, statins, theophylline
Timing nuance: enzyme induction is delayed (days–weeks — requires new enzyme synthesis); inhibition is rapid (hours).
Macrolides + statins: macrolides inhibit CYP3A4 → ↑ statin levels → myopathy and rhabdomyolysis. Check CK if muscle pain develops. Same applies to azole antifungals + statins.
Pharmacodynamics
📷 Image placeholder — Log dose–response curves — potency (leftward EC50 shift) vs efficacy (Emax height), overlaying full agonist, partial agonist, competitive antagonist and inverse agonist
🎯
Affinity
How well drug binds to receptor. Electrostatic = weak + reversible. Covalent = strong + irreversible (aspirin-COX, PPIs-ATPase).
📊
Efficacy vs Potency
Efficacy = maximal effect at max dose (Emax). Potency = dose needed to reach EC50. A drug can be highly potent (small dose effective) but low efficacy (small maximum effect).
🔬
Selectivity vs Specificity
Selectivity = for specific receptor (bisoprolol = β1-selective; celecoxib = COX-2 selective). Specificity = number of mechanisms (high specificity = one MOA; low = multiple → more SEs).
🔑
Agonist spectrum
Full agonist > partial agonist (submaximal effect even at full occupancy) > antagonist (binds, no effect — blocks agonist) > inverse agonist (binds, produces the opposite effect to the agonist).
Drug Interactions
Pharmacodynamic Interactions
  • Antagonism: beta-blocker + beta-agonist; naloxone + morphine
  • Augmentation (↑ bleeding): warfarin + NSAIDs, aspirin + clopidogrel
  • Augmentation (diuretics): furosemide + thiazides → profound hypokalaemia
  • Serotonin syndrome: SSRIs + tramadol or MDMA or St John's Wort → tremor, limb jerking, hypertonia, dilated pupils, sweating, confusion
Pharmacokinetic Interactions
  • Absorption: PPIs/antacids reduce absorption (clopidogrel); prokinetics reduce drug dwell time; antidiarrhoeal agents increase it
  • Distribution (protein-binding displacement): quinidine displaces digoxin → toxicity; warfarin displaced by sulfonamides → ↑ free warfarin → bleeding
  • Metabolism: CYP450 inducers/inhibitors (see above)
  • Elimination: NSAIDs reduce methotrexate excretion (severe toxicity); verapamil/quinidine/amiodarone reduce digoxin excretion
Adverse Drug Reactions (ADRs) — Types
A
Augmented (most common)
Exaggeration of normal pharmacological action. Dose-dependent. Primary (intended site): aspirin → bleeding. Secondary (off-target): bisoprolol → bronchospasm.
B
Bizarre (2nd most common)
Novel, unexpected response. Often immune-mediated/idiosyncratic. Not dose-dependent. Examples: Reye's syndrome (aspirin), penicillin anaphylaxis, carbamazepine → SJS, G6PD-related haemolysis (e.g. with primaquine, sulfonamides, nitrofurantoin).
C
Continued (chronic)
Persists long after stopping. Dose/time-dependent. Corticosteroids → osteoporosis; bisphosphonates → jaw osteonecrosis.
D
Delayed
Appears later, unpredictable. Not dose/time-dependent. Thalidomide → teratogenicity; antipsychotics → tardive dyskinesia.
E
End-of-use (Withdrawal)
Requires tapering not stopping: BZDs (agitation, seizures), corticosteroids (adrenal insufficiency), opioids (flu-like withdrawal), beta-blockers (rebound tachycardia).
Yellow Card Scheme: Voluntary reporting of suspected ADRs to MHRA. Anyone can report — no proof needed. Drugs with ▼ (black triangle) are newly licensed and under intensive monitoring. Particularly important for new drugs and vaccines.
⭐ Exam Pearls
Zero-order kinetics drugs: PASTA (Phenytoin, Aspirin, Salicylates, Theophylline, Alcohol). Risk: small dose increase → disproportionately large rise in drug concentration → toxicity.
Narrow therapeutic index → TDM: digoxin, lithium, phenytoin, theophylline, gentamicin/vancomycin, warfarin (INR), ciclosporin/tacrolimus.
Steady state: achieved after 4–5 half-lives regardless of route or dose. Loading dose set by Vd, maintenance dose by clearance. Loading dose bypasses the wait for rapid effect (digoxin, phenytoin).
Enzyme induction is delayed (days–weeks, new enzyme synthesis); inhibition is rapid (hours) — so an inhibitor causes toxicity quickly, an inducer causes failure slowly.
Rifampicin induction: reduces levels of warfarin, COCP, ciclosporin, statins. Turns secretions orange — warn patients (tears, urine, sweat).

Paracetamol Overdose
Causes hepatotoxicity via NAPQI (toxic metabolite). Higher risk in: chronic alcohol use, anorexia/malnutrition, P450 inducers, malnutrition (↓ glutathione). Features: initially asymptomatic, then N/V, RUQ pain, then jaundice + encephalopathy.
💊
Paracetamol Treatment
<1h: activated charcoal (↓ absorption). Staggered intake: IV acetylcysteine over 1 hour regardless. Non-staggered: <4h = monitor at 4h with nomogram; 4–8h = N-acetylcysteine if OD >150mg/kg; >24h with liver damage: N-AC. Transplant if: pH <7.3 after 24h OR all 3 of (PT >100s + creatinine >300 + grade 3/4 encephalopathy).
💊
Salicylate (Aspirin) Overdose
Causes: respiratory alkalosis first (hyperventilation stimulates medulla) → metabolic acidosis (lactic acid accumulation). Sx: tinnitus, hyperventilation, lethargy, sweating, pyrexia, N/V, seizures. Tx: activated charcoal if <1h. IV NaHCO3 (urinary alkalisation → ↑ salicylate excretion). Haemodialysis if: concentration >700mg/L, met acidosis, ARF, pulmonary oedema, seizures.
💊
Opioid Overdose
Classic triad: pinpoint pupils + respiratory depression + drowsiness. Also: rhinorrhoea, needle track marks, yawning, watering eyes. Emergency: IV/IM naloxone (opioid receptor antagonist — short-acting, may need repeat doses). Detoxification: methadone or buprenorphine substitution.
💊
TCA (Tricyclic) Overdose
Anticholinergic sx: dry mouth, dilated pupils, agitation, blurred vision, urinary retention, ileus. ECG: sinus tachycardia, wide QRS, prolonged QTc (risk torsades). Cardiotoxic — leads to arrhythmia. Treatment: activated charcoal if <1h. IV sodium bicarbonate (1st line) — alkalinise plasma → reduces free TCA, narrows QRS.
💊
BZD Overdose
Usually managed supportively. Flumazenil (GABA-A receptor antagonist) — reversal agent. Caution: may precipitate withdrawal seizures in dependent patients.
💨
Carbon Monoxide Poisoning
Confusion + headache + low-grade pyrexia. Pink mucosae (CO-Hb is bright red — misleading). SpO2 falsely normal (oximetry can't distinguish CO-Hb). Tx: 100% O2 via non-rebreathe mask (shortens CO-Hb t½ from 5h to 90min). Hyperbaric O2 if severe/pregnancy.
💨
Organophosphate Poisoning
Inhibit acetylcholinesterase → ACh excess. SLUD: Salivation, Lacrimation, Urination, Defaecation. Also: bradycardia, hypotension, miosis (small pupils), bronchospasm, seizures. Treatment: atropine 1st line (compete with ACh at muscarinic receptors — titrate until secretions dry). Pralidoxime (regenerates AChE) if given early.
🍸
Ethylene Glycol Poisoning
Found in antifreeze. Initial: CNS depression (ataxia, vomiting, dysarthria). Delayed: metabolic acidosis with raised anion gap (converted to oxalic acid → renal failure). Treatment: fomepizole (alcohol dehydrogenase inhibitor — 1st line) or ethanol infusion (competes for same enzyme) + haemodialysis.
🍸
Methanol Poisoning
Like ethylene glycol (same fomepizole / ethanol + haemodialysis) and a raised anion-gap metabolic acidosis — but the hallmark is visual loss / blindness (optic nerve toxicity from formic acid). Pair the two: glycol → renal failure, methanol → blindness.
🧲
Iron Overdose
Classic paediatric accidental OD. Phases: GI (vomiting, haematemesis, diarrhoea) → latent phase → shock + hepatotoxicity (later: bowel strictures). Antidote = desferrioxamine (chelator). Charcoal doesn't bind iron.
💊
Lithium Toxicity
Narrow TI. Tremor → coarse tremor, ataxia, confusion, seizures, renal impairment. Precipitated by dehydration, NSAIDs, ACEi, thiazides. No specific antidote — IV fluids (0.9% saline); haemodialysis if severe. (Cross-ref TDM/PK note.)
💉
Local Anaesthetic Toxicity
Perioral tingling, tinnitus, seizures, cardiac arrest (e.g. inadvertent IV bupivacaine). Antidote = IV lipid emulsion (Intralipid).
☠️
Cyanide Poisoning
Smoke inhalation (house fires) / industrial. Headache, ↓GCS, high lactate, cardiovascular collapse; classic bitter-almond smell. Antidote = hydroxocobalamin (or dicobalt edetate).
🧠
Serotonin Syndrome
Excess serotonergic activity. Common: SSRI + tramadol/MDMA/St John's Wort. Sx: tremors, limb jerking, clonus, hypertonia, dilated pupils, sweating, confusion, hyperthermia. Treatment: supportive (IV fluids, BZDs for agitation). Severe: cyproheptadine (5-HT2 antagonist) or chlorpromazine.

⭐ Exam Pearls
Paracetamol overdose: apparently well in first 24h but liver damage peaks at 72–96h. Early N-AC saves lives. Measure at 4 hours with nomogram (not earlier — unreliable).
Toxidrome "wet vs dry": cholinergic = wet + small pupils (organophosphates); anticholinergic = dry + large pupils (TCA/antihistamine). The single highest-yield discriminator.
Dialysable poisons: salicylates, lithium, methanol, ethylene glycol, theophylline. Charcoal is useless for metals, alcohols, and lithium.
Hyperthermia syndromes: serotonin syndrome = clonus/hyperreflexia/mydriasis; NMS = lead-pipe rigidity/bradyreflexia (antipsychotics); anticholinergic = dry/flushed/normal reflexes (cross-ref PK/PD note).
CO poisoning: SpO2 is falsely normal — co-oximetry needed for true O2 saturation. Cherry-red skin is a late/post-mortem finding, not reliable clinically.
TCA: wide QRS on ECG = cardiac toxicity. Sodium bicarbonate narrows QRS and prevents arrhythmia. Do NOT give flumazenil (might coexist with BZD; seizure risk).
Methanol → blindness; ethylene glycol → renal failure — both treated with fomepizole/ethanol + dialysis. Iron → desferrioxamine; LA toxicity → Intralipid; cyanide → hydroxocobalamin.
Opioid overdose vs BZD overdose: both cause CNS + respiratory depression. Opioid = pinpoint pupils; BZD = normal/large pupils. Naloxone reverses opioids; flumazenil reverses BZDs.
Aspirin overdose: mixed acid-base disorder — early respiratory alkalosis (aspirin stimulates medullary centre), then metabolic acidosis. Urinary alkalisation (NaHCO3) traps ionised salicylate in urine for excretion.

Palliative Care — Principles & Framework
What palliative care is (WHO): holistic care focused on quality of life in life-limiting illness — physical, psychological, social, spiritual. Not just end-of-life — it can run alongside active treatment.
The MDT

Anticipatory ("just in case") prescribing — the highest-yield concept
Four core end-of-life medications prescribed in advance for the dying patient (usually via syringe driver / CSCI):
  • Opioid (pain / breathlessness) — e.g. morphine
  • Antiemetic — e.g. haloperidol / levomepromazine / cyclizine
  • Antisecretory — hyoscine (hydrobromide/butylbromide) or glycopyrronium (secretions / "death rattle")

Morphine — Dosing Rules
Breakthrough dose = total daily opioid dose ÷ 6. E.g. morphine 30mg BD → breakthrough = (60)÷6 = 10mg. If not controlled → increase daily dose by 30–50%. If renal impairment → switch to oxycodone (not morphine — active metabolites accumulate).
🔄
Opioid Conversion
Oral → subcutaneous: divide total daily dose by 2. Oral morphine → subcutaneous diamorphine: divide by 3. Codeine → morphine: divide by 10. Always reassess pain after any dose change.
Opioid Toxicity
Signs: drowsiness, confusion, myoclonus, pinpoint pupils, respiratory depression. Action: reduce dose / rotate opioid + ensure hydration. Naloxone only if life-threatening respiratory depression (small titrated doses — avoid precipitating severe pain/withdrawal).
💨
Breathlessness
Low-dose opioids (morphine) ± benzodiazepine for the anxiety component. Non-drug measures: handheld fan, positioning, reassurance. Treat reversible causes (effusion, anaemia).
💩
Constipation
Near-universal with opioids → ALWAYS co-prescribe a laxative (the key prescribing-safety point): stimulant (senna) ± softener/osmotic (macrogol/docusate). Avoid bulk-forming laxatives in the dying patient.
😣
Agitation / Terminal Restlessness
Midazolam (first-line, via syringe driver); haloperidol or levomepromazine as alternatives. Completes the anticipatory-prescribing set. Exclude reversible causes (urinary retention, pain, constipation).
💊
Hyoscine Hydrobromide
Muscarinic antagonist. 1st line for: respiratory secretions ('death rattle') and bowel colic in palliation. Via syringe driver SC.
💊
Antiemetics in Palliation
Intracranial causes: cyclizine 1st line (H1 receptor antagonist — acts on vomiting centre). GI dysmotility: metoclopramide (D2 antagonist — prokinetic). Chemo-/radiotherapy-induced: ondansetron (5-HT3 antagonist).
💊
Raised ICP Headache
Dexamethasone — reduces peritumoural oedema in brain mets/primary brain tumour. High dose initially then taper to minimum effective dose.
💊
Metastatic Bone Pain
Analgesics (WHO pain ladder) + bisphosphonates (zoledronate — reduces skeletal events) + radiotherapy (single fraction for bone mets). Pathological fracture: orthopaedic surgery then radiotherapy.
💊
Hiccups
Chlorpromazine or haloperidol — both D2 antagonists. Baclofen (GABA agonist) as alternative. Persistent hiccups in palliative context often due to gastric distension, uraemia, or diaphragmatic irritation.
Routes of Administration
IV
Intravenous
100% bioavailability. Fastest onset (5–10 min). Not affected by first-pass metabolism. Risk: infection, phlebitis, air embolism. Volume limits: theoretically unlimited but practically titrated.
IM
Intramuscular
100% bioavailability. Max volume 5ml. Contraindicated in haemophilia (risk of massive haematoma). Examples: adrenaline, glucagon, vaccines.
SC
Subcutaneous
100% bioavailability. Max volume 2ml. Slower absorption than IM. Used in syringe drivers (palliation), insulin, LMWH, GLP-1 agonists.
SL
Buccal/Sublingual
Bypasses first-pass metabolism. Fast absorption. Examples: GTN (angina), buprenorphine, midazolam (seizures). Oral = variable bioavailability (hepatic first-pass reduces drug availability by up to 90% for some drugs).
INH
Inhaled
Local effects: SABA, ICS, ipratropium. Systemic effects: volatile anaesthetics. Drugs modified to reduce systemic absorption (e.g. poorly soluble ICS in lung).
TOP
Topical / Transdermal
Local: creams, ointments. Systemic delivery if highly lipid-soluble: nicotine patches, fentanyl patches (palliative), oestrogen patches, GTN patch. Bypasses first-pass.
EP
Epidural/Intrathecal
Epidural: outside dura. Used for analgesia/anaesthesia. SEs: dural puncture headache, abscess, haematoma, hypotension. Intrathecal: within subarachnoid space. Used for analgesia and intrathecal chemotherapy.
PR
Rectal/Vaginal
Rectal: fast onset (5–10 min), good for patients who can't take orally. Vaginal: less systemic absorption than rectal. Examples: diazepam PR (seizures), misoprostol PV, progesterone PV.
Fluid Prescribing
General prescribing reference — see the Fluid Therapy note (surgery module) for the full detail.
NICE Fluid Requirements
  • Water: 25–30 mL/kg/day
  • Electrolytes: 1 mmol/kg/day of Na, K, and Cl
  • Glucose: 50–100 g/day (caloric requirement)
  • Typical 70kg adult: 500mL 0.9% saline (+20mmol K+) + 1000mL 5% dextrose (+40mmol K+) per day
Resuscitation Fluid (Hypovolaemia)
  • Signs: BP <100/60, HR >90, cap refill >2s, RR >20, decreased O2 sats, ↓ urine output
  • Fluid challenge: 500ml crystalloid STAT (15 mins). Reduce to 250ml in elderly/HF/CKD.
  • Repeat up to 2000ml then seek senior review
  • Crystalloids: normal saline, Hartmann's (balanced — preferred to avoid hyperchloraemic acidosis)
  • Colloids (albumin): remain intravascular longer but risk of anaphylaxis — rarely used
K+ Administration
  • Never give K+ faster than 20 mmol/hour (risk of fatal cardiac arrhythmia)
  • Peripheral line: max 40 mmol/L concentration (causes thrombophlebitis if higher)
  • Central line: can give more concentrated K+ with continuous cardiac monitoring
